The abstract does not expose the final exact number, but the full-text conclusion is clear that the capability is learnable once the training distribution includes the right conditional structure.60:T405,GEASS (Gated Evidence-Aware Selective Steering) is plug-and-play and parameter-free:
- Two-path inference: run the model with the original prompt (clean path) and with an appended self-caption (caption path), producing two logit streams.
- Logit-level modulation using three signals:
  1) Confidence gate: uses the clean-path max probability as a proxy for whether external evidence is needed.
  2) Evidence-aware weight: measures caption usefulness via entropy reduction induced by the caption (information gain proxy).
  3) Selective disagreement penalty: when the two paths disagree, raise the threshold for letting the caption override, encoding the prior that captions mostly omit and occasionally fabricate (high-cost).
- Design choice: do not improve caption quality (no stronger captioner or external verification); instead, control the anchoring effect by regulating caption influence at the logits. Overhead is two additional forward passes per query, compatible with standard decoding as long as logits are accessible.61:T58a,TC-JEPA keeps the basic I-JEPA teacher-student structure. An online encoder processes visible context patches, an EMA target encoder provides target features for masked patches, and a predictor maps context plus mask tokens to predicted target representations.

The key change is in the predictor. Instead of compressing the caption into a single global text embedding, the model introduces a fine-grained text conditioner. At multiple predictor layers, target patch prediction is modulated through sparse cross-attention over text tokens. This lets each predicted patch selectively attend to relevant words and implicitly learn patch-word correspondences.

The paper also adds regularization on patch-word similarities, including sparsity and consistency constraints. The purpose is to prevent diffuse or unstable alignments across layers, so that text genuinely reduces uncertainty rather than becoming an extra noisy channel.

This differs from CLIP-style contrastive learning in a fundamental way. CLIP aligns whole-image and whole-text representations and often sacrifices local detail for semantic invariance. TC-JEPA keeps feature prediction as the training objective, so it has a better chance of preserving dense visual information while still injecting semantics. It also differs from prior patch-text correspondence work because the correspondence is learned to support prediction, not contrastive matching.62:T494,The paper reports that TC-JEPA improves over I-JEPA and several language-supervised contrastive baselines on classification, dense prediction, and multimodal tasks, while also being more stable and scalable during training. The provided excerpt does not include the full numeric tables, but the qualitative pattern is already informative.

Two claims matter most. First, dense prediction improves, which suggests that text conditioning does not simply push the representation toward coarse global semantics. This decomposition is useful because it localizes where failures may arise: graph encoding, projection/alignment, instruction understanding, or their interaction.

On top of that, the authors propose GTEval, an evaluation pipeline designed to probe graph-token understanding through instruction transformations rather than through new downstream tasks. The key idea is to vary instructions along two axes. The conclusion is nuanced: graph tokens are not ignored, and they do preserve task-relevant textual and structural information, but the way LLMs use them is unstable and often fails to generalize properly under instruction variation.

The authors further study extra instruction tuning and compare against Graph-Textualizing LLMs (GTextLLMs). The main findings are fourfold.

First, current GTokenLLMs do not fully understand graph tokens. Under format-level instruction changes, some models show large performance swings, indicating oversensitivity to prompt form. Under content-level changes, they can also be insufficiently responsive, indicating that they are not truly combining instruction semantics with graph-token semantics.

Second, these models rely heavily on textual attributes for reasoning, while their use of structural information is less robust. In other words, graph tokens may encode both text and topology, but the text component often dominates actual decision-making.

Third, attention and representation analyses show that graph tokens are not simply ignored. They are attended to across layers and retain task-relevant information. The problem is that their utilization patterns vary substantially across models and instruction variants, which points to weak and unstable semantic alignment.

Fourth, extra instruction tuning only partially helps. It improves performance on the original prompt and on seen instruction variants, but generalization to unseen transformations remains limited. That suggests the models are learning prompt adaptation more than genuine graph-token understanding.

For a foundation-model reader, the most useful part is not the absolute benchmark gain, but how reward design and CoT quality control affect downstream training signals.6a:T5c2,EOSTok is an end-to-end one-dimensional semantic tokenizer. Architecturally, it follows the TiTok-style 1D ViT autoencoder. Image patches are flattened and concatenated with L learnable query tokens, then passed through a causal ViT encoder. The encoder produces hidden patch embeddings and a 1D latent sequence z; only the query-token latents are kept as the image representation. Quantization uses an IBQ codebook with a straight-through estimator, and the decoder reconstructs the image from the quantized 1D tokens zq together with patch mask tokens. The important change is the training objective. In addition to standard tokenizer losses such as L1/L2 reconstruction, perceptual loss, GAN loss, and quantizer regularization, EOSTok jointly trains the tokenizer with an AR generator. The paper further adds Autoregressive Prediction Reconstruction loss. APR decodes the teacher-forced predictions of the AR model back into pixel space and applies a reconstruction loss there, so errors made by the AR model are fed back to the tokenizer through the final image domain. For semantic supervision, the paper avoids directly aligning the 1D latent sequence to 2D vision-foundation-model features, because that would push the sequence back toward raster-ordered patch alignment. Instead, it aligns the encoder's hidden patch embeddings to VFM representations, injecting semantic information while keeping the final latent sequence free from an explicit 2D layout constraint.6b:T40c,Read this one carefully. (1) Stochastic Condition Masking, SCM. During training, the aligned modality set is randomly partitioned into clean conditions and noisy targets. The targets are generated through the diffusion denoising process, while the conditions are provided as observed inputs. This forces the same text-to-video backbone to handle text-only, visual-only, and hybrid conditioning, instead of specializing to a fixed mapping. The key point is that the task definition itself is randomized, so one model can cover Text→X, X→X, and Text&X→X. (2) Decoupled Gated LoRA, DGL. Different modalities have different output distributions. Sharing one adapter across them causes interference, while full fine-tuning risks damaging the pretrained video prior. The paper assigns an independent LoRA to each modality and activates it only when that modality is a generation target. Condition modalities do not trigger their LoRA branches. This keeps adaptation localized to the output side that actually needs distributional adjustment. (3) Cross-Modal Self-Attention, CMSA. The model shares keys and values across modalities while keeping modality-specific queries. Shared K/V encourages all modalities to read from a common spatiotemporal context, improving alignment; separate Q preserves modality-specific retrieval behavior. Compared with fully separate attention, this increases dense cross-modal interaction. Compared with fully shared attention, it retains modality specificity. The framework is instantiated in two domains: UniVid-Intrinsic for RGB plus intrinsic maps, and UniVid-Alpha for blended RGB, alpha, foreground, and background, both built on top of pretrained video diffusion models with limited adaptation data.6d:T438,The experimental story has three parts. First, it builds a 64-layer RVQ neural audio codec. Each RVQ layer quantizes the residual left by earlier layers, so lower layers encode coarse acoustic content and deeper layers add progressively finer detail. The design trades a deeper and potentially higher-fidelity discrete representation for a harder tokenizer training problem and a more expensive LM target. Second, generation is factorized into two stages in the same acoustic-token space. A backbone model generates full-track coarse tokens. A super-resolution model then fills in higher RVQ layers. The refinement operates at full-track scale and predicts in parallel over time, giving a fixed 62-step layer-wise refinement process at inference. Third, the paper introduces hybrid-attention training for the super-resolution model. The alignment objective uses causal attention to learn text/vocal ordering, while the layer-wise refinement objective uses full attention to exploit the whole audio context when reconstructing fine tokens. Initializing the super-resolution model from the trained backbone is another important detail, as it transfers coarse-structure priors into fine-token refinement.6f:Tbed,方法的主线很清楚：先定义 anime 生成里什么叫“对”，再让模型逐步摆脱物理先验，最后建立新的优劣判别标准。

第一部分是 Production Knowledge System。作者认为 anime 数据自身过于多样，不能指望模型从原始像素里自动归纳出稳定的艺术先验，所以先人为提供一个结构化中介。这个系统至少包含两层：一层是工业化制作 taxonomy，把片段分解到 Style、Motion、Camera、VFX 四个可控轴；另一层是 AniCaption，把视频片段转成更像导演指令的语言，而不是普通视频 caption。这里的关键不是“多写一点描述”，而是把监督信号从结果描述改成生产变量描述。论文还提到用 graph-based multimodal reasoning 辅助标注，说明它不是纯模板抽取，而是试图从画面、时序和语义关系里推断制作意图。配合 dual-channel conditioning，模型一边接收精确的生产控制，一边接收更开放的艺术意图，从而避免单一文本条件既要承担硬约束又要承担模糊风格表达的冲突。

第二部分是 progressive style-motion-deformation curriculum。这是全文最像训练方法创新的地方。作者把 anime 相对自然视频的偏离拆成三条轴：风格多样性、运动幅度、形变强度。直接把高形变、高风格方差样本混进训练，会让已有物理 prior 与目标分布冲突过大，出现早期 collapse。于是他们采用渐进式课程，让模型先在更接近物理、风格更收敛、形变更弱的子分布上适应，再逐步扩大到更极端的表达。这个设计比常见的按分辨率或噪声级别 curriculum 更贴近 domain gap 的来源。它隐含的判断是：anime 迁移的难点不是单一复杂度，而是多个偏离维度叠加后导致优化面骤变，因此需要分轴控制训练路径。

第三部分是 deformation-aware preference optimization。作者指出，标准视频指标如 FVD、CLIP score 会把“艺术性变形”和“坏掉的结构”都视作偏离自然分布，因此无法作为 anime 域的可靠质量信号。为此他们引入领域奖励模型，并做偏好优化，让模型学会在“允许变形”的前提下仍保持角色一致性、动作意图、镜头节奏和特效合理性。这里的价值不只在于加了 reward model，而在于 reward 的判别边界被重新定义：不是惩罚一切 physics violation，而是惩罚没有艺术意图支撑的失真。若全文给出了偏好数据构造、正负样本来源、以及 reward 与生成器联训或后训的细节，这部分会很值得细看。

与已有方法相比，AniSora 这类工作更多是在 physics-trained video backbone 上加控制模块；AnimeReward 则偏向用人类反馈做质量对齐。AniMatrix 的区别在于，它把问题前移到预训练目标和数据组织层面：控制、课程学习、偏好优化三者围绕同一个“artistic correctness”定义协同，而不是在原有 realism objective 上做局部修补。70:T498,Its relevance to pretraining is broader than the anime setting. First, it makes a useful point about prior mismatch: a foundation video model trained under a realism objective may be systematically misaligned with domains whose structure is governed by production conventions rather than physical laws. That matters for stylized video, synthetic worlds, game footage, UI interaction video, and potentially multimodal generative models that mix natural and non-natural data. Second, the paper does not treat the issue as a simple fine-tuning problem. It proposes a full transition recipe: redefine supervision, bridge the prior gap with curriculum, then rebuild quality signals with domain-aware preference optimization. That is a meaningful template for domain adaptation under severe objective mismatch. Third, the move from descriptive captions to production-oriented directives is conceptually aligned with a larger trend in pretraining: replacing surface-level reconstruction targets with latent factor or process-level supervision. The contribution is less about a single algorithmic trick and more about a coherent training framework for a difficult target distribution.71:Tcef,The method is organized around a three-step transition: define artistic correctness, progressively override the inherited physics prior, and then distinguish valid artistic deformation from failure.

The first component is the Production Knowledge System. The authors argue that raw anime data is too diverse for a stable implicit prior to emerge on its own, so they introduce structured supervision. This includes an industrial production taxonomy that factorizes clips along four controllable axes: Style, Motion, Camera, and VFX. On top of that, they build AniCaption, which is not a standard captioner describing visible content, but a system that infers production variables and verbalizes them as creator- or director-like instructions. This is an important shift. The conditioning signal is no longer “what is in the clip,” but “how the clip should be authored.” The paper also mentions graph-based multimodal reasoning in the annotation pipeline, suggesting that the labels are inferred from relations across frames, semantics, and visual cues rather than extracted from a flat template. A dual-channel conditioning interface then separates precise production control from more flexible artistic intent, which likely reduces the burden on a single text channel to encode both hard constraints and soft style cues.

The second component is a progressive style-motion-deformation curriculum. This appears to be the main training innovation. The gap between natural-video priors and extreme anime expression is decomposed into three axes: style diversity, motion amplitude, and deformation intensity. Instead of mixing all anime samples at once, which the authors claim leads to early collapse, training proceeds through a controlled schedule that gradually increases difficulty along these axes. The rationale is strong: the optimization difficulty is not just “harder samples,” but a compounded mismatch across multiple dimensions that each break the original prior in a different way. A curriculum aligned with the source of domain shift is more principled than generic curricula based only on resolution or noise level.

The third component is deformation-aware preference optimization. Standard metrics such as FVD or CLIP-based similarity are poorly suited here because both intentional stylization and pathological corruption can look like deviations from natural video statistics. The paper therefore introduces a domain-specific reward model and uses preference optimization to teach the generator what counts as good anime deformation versus broken structure. The key idea is not merely adding a reward model, but redefining the reward boundary itself: physics violations are not uniformly bad; unsupported distortions are. If the full paper provides details on preference data construction, positive/negative pair generation, and how the reward model is integrated into training, that section is likely one of the most informative parts.

Compared with prior anime-generation work that mainly adds control modules or post-hoc alignment on top of physics-trained backbones, AniMatrix seems to intervene earlier, at the level of supervision design and optimization trajectory. Control, curriculum, and preference learning are all tied to the same target notion of artistic correctness.72:T8fa,The visible full-text excerpt does not include the complete experimental tables, so the strongest conclusions here are about evaluation design rather than all exact numbers. The paper is clearly set up to validate three claims.

First, it should compare against general-purpose video models or straightforward anime fine-tuning baselines. The expected result is that physics-biased models produce smoother but artistically flattened motion, while AniMatrix better preserves exaggerated action, impact framing, and style-specific expression. For this paper, subjective evaluation and domain-specific quality judgments matter more than generic video metrics alone.

Second, the curriculum should be tested through ablations. This is likely the most important experimental section. The paper needs to show that the three-axis curriculum specifically reduces early collapse, rather than any sample ordering giving similar gains. Useful evidence would include more stable training curves, better structural consistency as sample difficulty increases, and clear degradation when removing style, motion, or deformation progression. Direct mixed training should ideally show collapse modes or severe artifact rates.

Third, the reward model and preference optimization need to demonstrate that they can distinguish intentional exaggeration from failure better than generic metrics or judges. The most convincing evidence would be pairwise preference win rates, human evaluation, or stratified analysis across different deformation intensities. It is also important to check whether preference optimization improves quality without hurting controllability.

A full careful read is likely a 60–90 minute paper; for a targeted pass, prioritize the method overview, curriculum ablations, preference evaluation, and annotation examples in the appendix.74:T8b4,The method is a three-stage Draft-Evaluate-Diffuse pipeline. The novelty is less about any single component and more about how the three conditioning signals complement each other.

Stage 1 is Draft. Given a prompt p, the LLM generates a coarse visual draft d in the form of discrete vision tokens. This draft is not treated as the final image. It is a low-fidelity scene plan. The paper argues that this step is necessary because, without a concrete visual instance, later evaluation would collapse into generic prompt rewriting rather than grounded diagnosis.

Stage 2 is Evaluate. The same LLM takes the original prompt and the draft, compares them, and outputs a grounded evaluation e: a concise textual description of what is wrong or missing in the draft. This is the key move in the paper. The system exploits the empirical asymmetry that the unified model is better at post hoc diagnosis than at one-shot generation. Instead of asking the model to satisfy all constraints directly, it first asks it to create something inspectable and then to critique that object.

Stage 3 is Diffuse. A frozen SANA diffusion model is conditioned jointly on (p, d, e). The prompt provides the global semantic target, the draft provides a spatial anchor and scene layout, and the evaluation provides localized corrective instructions. The paper repeatedly argues that these signals are complementary: draft alone would preserve its own mistakes, evaluation alone without a visual anchor would reduce to prompt rewriting, and prompt alone returns to the standard text-conditioned diffusion setup.

Relative to prior work, this is not just prompt enhancement, because the evaluation is grounded in a specific visual draft. It is also different from generic coarse-to-fine generation, because the refinement signal is explicit language feedback rather than an implicit latent refinement path. From a pretraining perspective, the method also encodes a practical division of labor: the LLM handles discrete planning and semantic verification, while diffusion handles high-fidelity rendering. That division is more realistic than expecting one model to jointly master fine-grained pixel synthesis and compositional reasoning at the same level.75:T6e6,The main empirical result is clear: with the same frozen SANA diffusion backbone, UniReasoner improves prompt faithfulness rather than merely image quality. The headline numbers reported in the paper are 0.79 to 0.88 on GenEval, an absolute gain of 0.09, and 84.50 to 86.30 on DPG-Bench, a gain of 1.8 points. The larger signal on GenEval is especially important because that benchmark stresses compositional alignment.

The paper also provides qualitative evidence for the central hypothesis. Typical examples include counting failures where the model generates five apples for a prompt asking for four, yet correctly identifies the mismatch when asked to evaluate the generated image. Similar patterns appear for spatial relations and physical plausibility. These examples matter because they validate the claimed asymmetry directly, rather than relying only on benchmark aggregates.

The most important ablations are the conditioning variants: prompt only, prompt plus draft, prompt plus evaluation, and prompt plus both. The paper’s argument is that the full combination works best because draft and evaluation carry different information: visual anchoring versus explicit correction. Draft alone can lock the generator into the draft’s mistakes; evaluation alone lacks a concrete spatial reference. Even though the provided excerpt does not include every table entry, the logic of the ablation and the reported gains strongly suggest that the improvement comes from complementary conditioning rather than from simply adding more tokens.

Another important design choice is the frozen generator. Since SANA is not retrained, the gains can be attributed mainly to the reasoning and conditioning interface, which makes the result cleaner and more transferable.76:T4fb,Start with the introduction and the motivating example around the understanding-generation gap. That example is the paper’s foundation. If the asymmetry feels real, the rest of the design becomes easy to follow.

Then read the method section with one question in mind: why is grounded evaluation necessary, instead of plain prompt rewriting or self-refinement text? The answer defines the paper’s real contribution. The draft is not there for quality; it is there to create an inspectable object. The evaluation is not there to paraphrase the prompt; it is there to produce actionable corrections tied to that object.

In the experiments, prioritize two things. First, the main benchmark tables on GenEval and DPG-Bench, especially where the gains concentrate. Second, the ablations and failure cases when draft or evaluation is removed. Those parts reveal the role of each conditioning signal.

And can the single-pass pipeline be extended into a multi-round draft-critique-refine loop? Those are the places where the idea could evolve into a broader training or inference framework.77:T570,CIRM (Causal Intervention for Reward Models) performs neuron-level interventions during RM inference.
- Bias specification: define several measurable bias attributes f_b(x) for a query-response pair x (the paper studies five style-related biases, including length, paragraphing, exclamation marks, and lexical overlap).
- Neuron identification: for each bias b, compute correlations between intermediate neuron activations (typically MLP neurons across layers) and f_b(x) over a dataset; select a small set of “bias-specific neurons” with highest correlation.
- Inference-time intervention: clamp those neurons’ activations to their median values (per neuron) rather than zeroing them out. Median clamping is a distribution-preserving suppression that aims to remove bias signal while avoiding out-of-distribution activations that could harm general reward quality.
- Multi-bias handling: because neurons are selected per attribute, multiple bias interventions can be applied together.
- Mechanistic note: bias-specific neurons are reported to concentrate in early layers, implying the RM extracts format/style cues early and later mixes them with semantic signals.
Compared to prior inference-time debiasing that mostly applies scalar reward corrections based on response length, CIRM operates in representation space and is designed to generalize across different stylistic shortcuts.78:T67b,The framework has three main components. First, the LaST-R1 architecture. It is initialized from Qwen3-VL-4B and further pretrained on large-scale robotic manipulation datasets. At inference time, the model autoregressively generates latent reasoning tokens before producing actions, and those latent tokens condition a parallel action decoder. These tokens are not natural-language explanations; they are internal reasoning representations intended to capture physical dynamics, future state structure, and manipulation intent. To stabilize them, the authors anchor the latent reasoning space to global future representations from a vision foundation model, providing semantic and spatial priors so the latent variables do not drift into arbitrary hidden codes. Second, LAPO, or Latent-to-Action Policy Optimization. Instead of applying PPO-style optimization only to action probabilities, LAPO defines a joint step-level likelihood ratio over latent reasoning and action generation. This allows environmental reward to influence both the internal reasoning trajectory and the final action policy. The key benefit is better credit assignment: the reward arrives from interaction outcomes, but the update can still reach the intermediate reasoning process. Third, the adaptive latent CoT mechanism. Rather than fixing a constant reasoning horizon, the model adjusts the amount of latent reasoning based on task demands. Harder tasks can allocate more internal computation, while reactive tasks can use shorter reasoning for lower latency. The overall training recipe is pretraining on robotic data, task-specific SFT warm-up, and then online RL post-training.79:T547,From the provided full-text excerpt, the main confirmed results are as follows: the model is built on Qwen3-VL-4B and pretrained on multiple robotic manipulation datasets; on LIBERO, it reaches a 99.8% average success rate with one-shot warm-up, outperforming prior baselines; on four real-world complex tasks, LAPO improves over the warm-up policy by up to 44%, reaching a 90% average success rate across single-arm and dual-arm settings; after RL post-training, the system also shows zero-shot generalization to unseen objects, backgrounds, and lighting conditions. The experimental story appears to have three pillars. First, comparisons against vanilla action-only RL policies show that jointly optimizing latent reasoning and actions improves robustness and generalization. Second, adaptive latent CoT is evaluated against fixed reasoning horizons, supporting the claim that reasoning depth should be task-dependent. Third, real-robot experiments indicate the gains are not confined to simulation. Even so, the intended claim is already clear: latent reasoning does not have to be learned only through imitation; it can be directly shaped by online RL.7a:T40a,A useful skim takes about 30 to 40 minutes. Start with Figure 1, which contrasts action-only RL with reasoning-before-acting RL; that figure captures the paper’s main thesis. If time is limited, skip detailed task descriptions and visual examples, and keep the algorithm equations, training pipeline figure, main result tables, and key ablations.7b:T64f,ANCORA uses a single shared policy that alternates between two roles: a Proposer that generates new specifications and a Solver that attempts verified solutions. The method has three main components.

The first is a two-level group-relative update. On the Solver side, the update is close to GRPO, but replaces standard-deviation normalization with mean normalization so that the gradient better matches the MLRL weighted-pass@k objective. This gives rare successful trajectories larger weight. On the Proposer side, advantages are defined over candidate specifications based on the distribution of Solver outcomes, with the aim of generating tasks near the Solver’s competence frontier rather than trivially easy or impossible ones.

The second is iterative self-distilled SFT. The authors argue that sparse-reward exploration alone causes the Proposer to drift away from the valid-output manifold. They therefore repeatedly project the model back onto a region that reliably produces valid specifications and solutions before full RL. This is presented as a stabilizing requirement, not a minor warm-start trick.

The third is a UCB-guided Curriculum DAG. Newly proposed tasks are admitted only if they pass strict filtering, novelty checks, and Solver verification. UCB is used to select seeds from the existing DAG, balancing exploration and exploitation while preventing curriculum poisoning.

Compared with standard self-improvement setups, the novelty is not the verifier itself but the closed-loop coupling of proposer learning, solver learning, manifold preservation, and controlled curriculum expansion.7c:T692,The method centers on the SciSense framework. Drawing from sensemaking theory, the authors decompose research ideation into eight ordered cognitive stages and use citation neighborhoods as conditioning context, producing full research trajectories rather than short proposals. The dataset, SciSense-Traj, has two modes. In Target mode, given a target paper and its cited works, the model reconstructs a plausible ideation trajectory that could have led from those citations to the known paper. In Infer mode, given the same citation context, the model proposes novel directions without anchoring to a known outcome. These trajectories are then distilled into SciSense-LM models ranging from 3B to 70B.

The most interesting part is not the eight-stage framework by itself, but the supervision design. Intuitively, open-ended Infer supervision might seem more creative. The paper finds the opposite: outcome-anchored Target supervision produces trajectories that are both higher quality and more diverse. The proposed mechanism is that Target trajectories spend more effort on constructive stages such as Schema and Elaboration, which organize prior work into a coherent explanatory structure, whereas Infer trajectories overemphasize early Hypothesis and Questioning stages, leading to broader but less grounded plans. In that sense, the constraint is not merely narrowing the search space; it provides a stabilizing structural prior for a difficult planning problem.

From a training perspective, this is best understood as trajectory distillation: generate structured research plans with a stronger process, then transfer that planning behavior into smaller or more standard LLMs.7d:T50b,The main empirical result is consistent and simple: Target supervision beats Infer on both diversity and quality across model families and scales, without the usual quality–diversity tradeoff. The paper reports a 2.0% gain in aggregate plan quality for Target over Infer, while also showing stronger diversity under multiple automatic metrics. It also includes stage-level analysis showing that Target plans emphasize Schema and Elaboration, whereas Infer plans front-load Hypothesis and Questioning.

The downstream transfer result is more important than the planning metrics alone. When these trajectories are used to condition coding agents, Target trajectories improve the quality of generated scientific artifacts, especially scientific grounding, and also help executability and downstream utility. That suggests the planning text is not decorative; it changes downstream agent behavior in measurable ways.

In terms of scale, the dataset is around 100K trajectories and the distilled models span 3B to 70B. When reading the full experiments, the main things to verify are whether the diversity metrics capture semantic diversity rather than surface variation, whether human and automatic evaluations agree, and whether the downstream gains are robust across tasks and model choices.7e:T663,AdaMeZO keeps the SPSA/MeZO gradient estimator as the base primitive. At each step, it perturbs parameters along a random direction z_t, computes a finite-difference loss projection from forward passes, and reconstructs the update direction using the same pseudorandom seed. The challenge is that Adam requires m_t and v_t, two full-size state vectors.

The key idea is to replace exact persistent moments with truncated, reconstructable approximations. First, AdaMeZO uses truncated first- and second-moment estimates rather than full EMAs over the entire optimization history. Older gradients are discarded, motivated by the fact that EMA already downweights them exponentially and their contribution is small relative to recent noisy zeroth-order estimates.

Second, the method exploits finer-grained PRNG replay. Instead of materializing full random directions globally, it regenerates them block by block. This allows the optimizer to reconstruct local pieces of the recent moment history on demand from stored scalar projections and PRNG seeds, rather than storing full moment tensors. In effect, it trades lightweight recomputation for memory.

This is the main distinction from prior adaptive ZO methods. HiZOO explicitly approximates diagonal Hessian information. Helene is closer to a direct Adam-style ZO optimizer with explicit state. AdaMeZO instead focuses on eliminating optimizer-state residency while preserving most of the benefit of preconditioning. The paper also provides a non-convex convergence result showing that the rate recovers that of preconditioned MeZO up to approximation terms introduced by truncation.7f:T444,The experiments are designed to show both optimization behavior and practical LLM tuning gains. On 2D toy landscapes, the optimization trajectories illustrate the intended effect clearly: AdaMeZO follows more stable paths toward minima, while MeZO is more prone to oscillation or poor convergence under the same step budget.

The main empirical section fine-tunes RoBERTa, OPT, and LLaMA on the same task suite used by MeZO, which makes the comparison clean. The headline result is efficiency rather than just end accuracy: AdaMeZO almost always reaches the same stopping criterion as MeZO with up to 70% fewer forward passes, while also delivering better final task performance. That matters because forward evaluations are the dominant cost in zeroth-order tuning.

The most informative ablations are the ones around truncation length, block-wise reconstruction granularity, and the stability of gains across model families. The paper’s claim is not merely that adaptive scaling helps, but that most of the benefit can be retained without paying the usual memory cost of Adam-like states.80:T53c,Two-stage design:
1) Task-vector analysis. Define task vectors as Δθ between a post-trained checkpoint and the base model. The paper reports three structural properties:
- Magnitude disparity: SFT task vectors have ~30× larger L2 norms than RLVR across layers, so naive linear merging is dominated by SFT.
- Sign interference: ~44.91% of parameters have opposite signs between the two vectors, explaining persistent gradient conflicts in joint training.
- Module-wise heterogeneity: SFT concentrates “important” updates in LayerNorm (reported ~19.9%), whereas RLVR spreads updates across attention, LayerNorm, and the LM head, suggesting partial complementarity.
2) DoTS (Decoupled Test-time Synthesis). Train SFT and RLVR separately, then synthesize at inference: θ = θ0 + λ_sft Δθ_sft' + λ_rlvr Δθ_rlvr'.
- Selective sparsification: keep only top-k% coordinates by magnitude in each task vector, zero the rest, then rescale to preserve the original norm. This is positioned as the key fix for both magnitude imbalance and sign conflicts, reducing sign interference from 44.91% down to as low as ~7.1%.
- Coefficient search: use Bayesian optimization over two scalars (λ_sft, λ_rlvr) on a small set of unlabeled queries, guided by proxy signals such as consistency and perplexity. No parameter updates; only scalar tuning.81:T542,The paper’s logic is:
1) Underspecification of RLVR: with binary verifier reward R(x,y)∈{0,1}, the objective is equivalent to maximizing Zθ(x)=∑_{y∈C(x)} πθ(y|x). Any policy with the same Zθ(x) is equally optimal, regardless of whether it is fully collapsed or maximally diverse over correct outputs.
2) Collapse via training dynamics: in GRPO, for each prompt, K rollouts are sampled; all correct samples share the same positive advantage A+ (and all incorrect share A-). This means gradients preferentially amplify whichever correct solutions are sampled more often, which increases their sampling probability, creating a positive feedback loop that suppresses alternative correct solutions.
3) What the optimum should be: they define two criteria—robustness under distribution shift and entropy-regularized optimality—and show both select the same structure: the Uniform-Correct Policy (zero mass on incorrect outputs, uniform distribution over all correct outputs).
They then propose Uniform-Correct Policy Optimization (UCPO), a modification of GRPO that adds a uniformity term over correct solutions, reallocating gradient signal from dominant correct outputs toward underrepresented ones. They prove the Uniform-Correct Policy is the unique optimum of UCPO (Theorem 6.1), addressing the original objective’s indifference.82:T7ca,The paper first reviews several diversity-oriented SFT objectives, including standard CE, distribution-preserving alternatives, and regularized variants. The central claim is that fixing only one side of the problem is insufficient. If one only emphasizes rare patterns, the model may still forget the pretrained distribution. If one only preserves the base model distribution, head patterns in the supervised data still dominate learning. This motivates TOFU, a Tempered Focal loss.

From the formulation and motivation described in the text, TOFU combines two ideas. The focal component downweights easy, already-high-probability targets so that hard tokens and low-frequency patterns receive stronger gradient signal. This addresses the tendency of instruction tuning to concentrate on a narrow set of dominant responses. The tempered component acts as a conservative update mechanism relative to the pretrained model, reducing excessive drift away from the base distribution and preserving alternative plausible continuations that are not explicitly present in the SFT data. In effect, TOFU tries to control two gradient sources at once: the sharp pull from one-hot supervision and the stabilizing pull from the reference model.

Relative to prior methods:
1. unlike plain CE, it does not treat all token errors equally and explicitly reallocates learning signal toward hard and tail events;
2. unlike plain focal loss, it is not only a difficulty-based reweighting scheme, because it also tries to retain pretrained knowledge;
3. unlike pure KL anchoring or distillation-style regularization, it is not uniformly conservative and still allows substantial updates where the supervised signal is genuinely corrective.

From a training-dynamics perspective, the method can be read as a more selective budget allocation rule: spend less update budget on high-frequency, low-information tokens, spend more on tail tokens, and use a tempered reference to avoid catastrophic distributional drift.83:T4e3,Based on the provided full-text excerpt, the authors run broad evaluations across model families, datasets, and benchmarks, compare existing diversity-oriented SFT objectives in a unified setup, and separately test focal loss as an SFT objective. The qualitative conclusion is that TOFU improves generative diversity over standard CE while keeping output quality competitive. Focal loss alone already helps with low-frequency pattern coverage, but without the tempered reference term it is not sufficient to reliably preserve pretrained knowledge.

However, the excerpt does not include the full experimental tables, model sizes, training-token counts, benchmark names, or exact numerical gains, so it would be unsafe to invent precise improvements. The robust takeaways are:
1. diversity collapse under standard SFT appears consistently across multiple settings rather than as a model-specific artifact;
2. quality-only evaluation can hide distributional narrowing, so diversity and quality must be measured jointly;
3. combining rare-pattern reweighting with reference preservation works better than either ingredient alone.

The paper shows that when the target capability is long-horizon, tool-using, evidence-sparse scientific reasoning, data construction becomes the central bottleneck. There are three concrete contributions. First, it proposes an automated task-construction framework tailored to frontier science rather than reusing general-domain information-seeking recipes. On the data side, the authors start from a curated pool of frontier scientific entities. They then build two pipelines. The first is a conceptual pipeline: a web agent browses academic sources starting from seed entities, gathers evidence, and generates grounded questions. Complexity is then increased through iterative anchor-based task augmentation, where an anchor is the decisive scientific entity that serves as the central handle for the question. The second is a computational pipeline: the system performs a three-level evidence selection process to identify scientific models associated with seed entities, including governing equations, mechanistic understanding, and required input parameters. It then generates computational questions and obtains reference answers through voting-based solver verification. The key idea is not merely to add arithmetic, but to supervise the full chain of finding the right model, extracting the right quantities, and executing the computation. These pipelines produce SciResearcherQA. On the training side, the authors follow a fairly standard but carefully executed deep-research post-training recipe on top of Qwen3-8B: supervised fine-tuning with rejection sampling, followed by reinforcement learning with GRPO, yielding SciResearcher-8B. A notable point is that RL is used not only to improve final accuracy but also to shape longer, more tool-intensive, and difficulty-adaptive trajectories. Rewards are divided by source into intrinsic and external rewards. Intrinsic rewards are then split into certainty-based and ensemble-based rewards. Certainty-based rewards use signals derived from the policy itself, such as token entropy, trajectory likelihood, sequence probability, self-certainty, or probability gaps over answer tokens. Examples include RLIF, EM-RL, RENT, RLSC, and RLSF. Ensemble-based rewards use agreement among multiple rollouts, with majority voting as the central case.

The technical core is the sharpening mechanism. For majority-style rewards, if an answer is already the majority under the initial sampling distribution, RL updates increase its probability further. For certainty-style rewards, the update favors outputs that the model already assigns high confidence to. The paper analyzes one-step dynamics and convergence, and then generalizes the argument through a unified reward framework in the appendix. The induced optimum is not the true answer distribution. It is a sharpened version of the model’s initial distribution.

This explains the main tradeoff. If the initial model prior is aligned with correctness, sharpening raises accuracy and consistency. If the prior is misaligned, the same training objective reinforces wrong answers. The paper also introduces model collapse step as a practical proxy for prior quality. A model that collapses later under intrinsic URLVR tends to have more usable prior structure and is more likely to benefit from RL.8c:T694,The experiments compare multiple intrinsic URLVR variants, including majority-voting methods and certainty-based rewards. The analysis tracks training dynamics rather than only final accuracy: answer distributions, majority stability, confidence metrics, collapse behavior, and per-problem sharpening are all used.

The first recurring pattern is early improvement followed by collapse. Early gains come from making initially correct majority answers more stable. Longer training reduces diversity and can reinforce wrong modes, which causes performance to degrade.

The second pattern is method-dependent failure. Majority-voting rewards fail when the sampled majority answer is wrong. Certainty-based rewards fail when the model is poorly calibrated and assigns high confidence to incorrect reasoning paths. In that case, entropy minimization or likelihood-based rewards turn overconfidence into the training target.

The third pattern is that constrained usage is safer. Small training sets reduce distribution drift and delay collapse. Test-time training is also safer because adaptation is local to a problem or a small batch of problems, making it closer to controlled sharpening of the current prior.

The fourth pattern is predictive: collapse step correlates with later RL gains. The paper studies different backbones, training stages, model scales, generation settings, and training datasets, and finds that resistance to collapse is an informative early signal. The provided full-content excerpt does not expose exact parameter counts, dataset sizes, or final numeric scores, so the reliable takeaway is the training-dynamics result rather than a specific benchmark number.8d:T474,The method has two stages. First, generate many candidate completions from the finetuned model. To induce diversity, the authors prepend short random prefills drawn from common public corpora, then decode with temperature zero. These prefills act as varied entry points that can trigger overgeneralized finetuned behavior outside its intended setting. Second, score each completion under both the finetuned model and a reference model, which can be the pre-finetuning checkpoint or a cross-family model. Completions are ranked by perplexity-based gaps, typically favoring text that is low perplexity for the finetuned model and high perplexity for the reference model. Such text is likely to reflect newly learned behavior, memorized training strings, or emergent side effects of finetuning. The method does not require internal activations or prior knowledge of the target behavior. The motivation is that many target tokens are stylistic, formatting-related, or otherwise substitutable, and forcing the base model to fit them equally can inject noisy updates that later merge poorly into the instruction model. It then motivates bounded JSD for stability in the former and reverse KL (mode-seeking) for coherence in the latter, claiming theoretical and empirical validation.92:T411,CoRD, or Collaborative Reasoning Decoding, treats each reasoning step as a high-level decoding unit. At each step, multiple teacher LRMs propose candidate next steps conditioned on the same current prefix. The system scores the resulting partial trajectories and extends promising ones. The method has three central components. First, prompt-guided step segmentation makes reasoning steps more consistent across teachers. Second, predictive perplexity scores a partial reasoning prefix by measuring how well the ground-truth answer is predicted given that prefix; this provides an early signal without waiting for a complete trace. Third, beam search maintains multiple candidate trajectories, which helps preserve paths that initially look weaker but later lead to useful self-correction or strategic shifts. Compared with S1- or LIMO-style curation, CoRD collaborates during generation rather than selecting after generation. Compared with PRM or MCTS-style methods, it avoids heavy rollout-based search and uses a decoding-like procedure.93:T5fb,The starting point is fixed-reference KL-regularized reward maximization: maximize expected verifier reward while penalizing KL from π_ref. The optimizer is a Boltzmann target policy, proportional to π_ref multiplied by exp(r/β), where β controls the strength of the KL regularizer. A weighted SFT objective, however, induces a policy proportional to q w, where q is the rollout sampler and w is the sample weight. Matching weighted SFT to the RLVR optimizer requires q w to equal the Boltzmann target, so w must be proportional to π*/q. In the reference-sampled case q = π_ref, this uniquely gives the prompt-normalized Boltzmann density ratio exp(r(x,y)/β) / Z(x). The proposed BOLT procedure precomputes reference rollouts, verifier scores, Monte Carlo normalizers, and Boltzmann weights, then trains with standard multi-epoch SFT. The finite-data analysis separates a support gap from ordinary learning errors. For a one-shot sampled set S_N, even the best support-restricted replacement pays β log(1 / π*(S_N | x)) if the sampled support misses target mass. Other terms include partition-function estimation error, effective-sample-size variance, empirical generalization, optimization error, and parametric approximation. In binary-verifier settings, rare correct samples create a temperature–coverage–variance tradeoff, with roughly 1/p reference samples needed when the reference pass probability is p. Refreshing the sampler by using the current policy as the next reference recovers KL policy mirror descent.94:T74d,The technical story has four steps. First, under a log-linear policy class, the authors show that flipping a single preference label induces a fixed shift in the DPO gradient that does not depend on the current parameter. This is the key simplification. It turns poisoning from a trajectory-dependent optimization in policy space into a subset-selection problem in gradient space, where each example contributes one dictionary atom corresponding to its flip-induced gradient shift.

Second, they show that controlling the residual in this gradient-space approximation is a sufficient surrogate for attack success in policy space. This reduces targeted poisoning to a structured binary sparse approximation problem: coefficients are binary because each label is either flipped or not; the goal is either to minimize the number of flips or to find the best attack under a budget K.

Third, they propose two algorithms. BAL-A targets the minimum-flip setting. It embeds the binary selection problem into a lattice with penalties for both approximation error and non-binary integer coefficients, then applies LLL basis reduction and Babai’s nearest-plane algorithm to recover an integer solution interpretable as a flip pattern. The paper analyzes how the embedding penalty controls the solution and gives a separation condition under which the true minimum-flip attack is recovered. BMP-A targets the sparse fixed-budget setting. It adapts Binary Matching Pursuit, using normalized correlations to handle non-uniform column norms in the gradient dictionary, and derives coherence-based recovery guarantees.

Fourth, the paper also provides simple robustness certificates: under certain geometric conditions on the dictionary, no K-flip attack can succeed. This is useful because it goes beyond attack construction and starts to characterize verifiable safety conditions.95:T523,The experiments are designed to validate the geometry and recovery theory rather than to maximize downstream task scores. Synthetic-dictionary experiments test two main claims. First, BAL-A is sharply sensitive to the lattice penalty, and successful recovery occurs only in the theoretically predicted penalty regime. Second, BMP-A behaves as expected from sparse recovery theory: lower dictionary coherence leads to substantially better attack recovery.

The real-data experiments build dictionaries from the Stanford Human Preferences (SHP) dataset. The point is not to run a full large-scale LLM DPO pipeline, but to test whether the gradient-space reduction remains meaningful on realistic preference data. The answer is largely yes. BAL-A shows a clear phase transition with respect to the penalty parameter on SHP, and BMP-A improves markedly when dictionary coherence is reduced. For this kind of paper, the important empirical result is not simply attack strength, but whether the theoretical reduction survives contact with real preference datasets. The experiments support that claim reasonably well.

First, it constructs a verified correct symbolic reasoning chain C+ using an LLM-plus-symbolic-prover setup similar in spirit to ProverGen. The chain is generated under rule templates and each step is checked for derivability, so only truth-consistent trajectories are kept. Second, it injects a template-aware error at an intermediate step k. The error type is constrained by the local rule template rather than sampled from a global noise process, which makes the corruption structurally compatible with the local inference pattern. Third, the corrupted step is treated as part of the new symbolic state, and all downstream steps are recomputed under that corrupted state to produce an erroneous chain C-. This is the key design choice: later steps remain consistent with the wrong prefix, instead of becoming unrealistic label-flipped artifacts. Fourth, the framework verifies that the injected step is truly the first invalid step. For non-structural errors, it performs a prefix non-derivability check; if the corrupted conclusion is still derivable from the prefix, the sample is rejected. For structural errors, it checks violations of rule direction, dependency order, or acyclicity constraints. Finally, both the correct and erroneous symbolic chains are translated into aligned natural-language processes under shared context, entity realizations, and predicate mappings, so the pair differs mainly in reasoning behavior rather than surface form.98:T542,The method has two main components. The first is data construction. Instead of asking a strong model to freely generate multi-hop QA pairs, the pipeline starts with hard example mining: identify questions or document regions that the current base agent fails on, then use a frontier model to mutate or expand them into new multi-hop questions. A filtering pipeline follows, with two key checks. One is factual grounding, which ensures the question and answer are supported by source documents rather than model hallucination. The other is retrieval-solvability, which tests whether the question remains answerable in a noisy but high-recall retrieval setting. This is an important design choice: the target is not maximal difficulty, but a learnable difficulty band where RL can improve policy behavior. The second component is reward design. In addition to final answer correctness, the paper introduces a retrieval-aware reward that explicitly scores search quality and evidence selection. From the full text, this is meant to provide denser credit assignment than a pure outcome reward, so the model can learn which search actions were actually productive. From the student side, it improves exploration with two balancing strategies. Offline difficulty-aware balancing shapes the training distribution by sample difficulty, so training is not dominated by trivial examples or by examples that are too hard to learn from. Online correctness-aware balancing then uses the student’s current rollout correctness to keep training focused on informative states, especially near the boundary between correct and incorrect behavior. From the teacher side, the paper introduces outcome-guided margin calibration. Vanilla OPD trusts the teacher’s token probabilities on student rollouts, but those rollouts can be out of distribution for the teacher. The proposed calibration uses outcome reward as a global anchor: after aggregating token-level teacher scores over a trajectory, correct trajectories should rank above incorrect ones by a margin. If this order consistency is violated, the teacher signal is adjusted. This is meant to handle teacher degradation on unusual student prefixes, fluent but wrong reasoning chains, conflicts between multiple teachers, and unstable multimodal supervision.9b:T543,The method decomposes evaluation into rubric generation and rubric-conditioned judging. A rubric is considered useful if it helps a judge assign a higher score to a preferred response than to a dispreferred one. Rubric quality is therefore directly trainable through discriminative utility, measured by the score gap induced by the rubric. The paper formulates rubrics as latent variables and derives a training objective from a variational-inference view. Training alternates between two phases. In the policy phase, a frozen rubric model generates rubrics for questions; the policy samples multiple responses; a frozen judge scores the responses under the rubric; GRPO updates the policy using these rubric-derived rewards. In the rubric phase, preference pairs are built through temporal contrast: current-policy responses are treated as preferred, earlier-checkpoint responses as dispreferred. The rubric generator samples candidate rubrics, and receives reward when the judge conditioned on that rubric separates the pair in the right direction with a larger gap. This differs from GPT-4.1-generated rubrics or labeled rubric training because it does not require an external rubric teacher. It uses a standard autoregressive model, a single context, and the same hidden-state evolution. The only addition is lightweight tagging that distinguishes two action types inside one token stream: think tokens and speak tokens. Think tokens update the context but are not disclosed to the user. Speak tokens are both part of the context and an early-released prefix of the final answer. The key constraint is not merely to speak early, but to speak only when the disclosed prefix is supported by the reasoning generated so far.

Training has two stages. The first is entailment-aligned interleaved supervision. Starting from ordinary triples (x, r, a), where r is reasoning and a is the final answer, the paper aligns answer prefixes with reasoning prefixes so that each early disclosure is justified by the available reasoning prefix. This is the central mechanism that avoids two degenerate solutions: unsupported early commitments and low-information filler text that improves superficial latency metrics without helping the user.

The second stage is SFT followed by RL. SFT teaches the model the semantics of the dual-action format and the pacing structure. But the paper argues that SFT alone is insufficient because the interleaved format changes the rollout distribution: the model may learn the format while losing some reasoning quality under the new commitment constraints. RL is then used to recover task performance and optimize the trade-off between correctness and content latency. In other words, RL is not just a score booster here; it helps the model re-adapt its reasoning policy under the new disclosure regime.

Relative to prior work, SxS differs from template-based interleaving because disclosure timing is learned rather than fixed. It differs from dual-channel or latent-reasoning systems because there is no separate hidden channel or second decoder. It also differs from system-level latency optimization because the target is supported content timing, not just earlier token emission.9e:T67f,The evaluation spans two Qwen3 architectures, one MoE and one dense, at two scales including 30B-A3B and 4B. The benchmarks are AIME25 for in-domain mathematical reasoning and GPQA-Diamond for out-of-domain scientific QA. Importantly, the paper does not evaluate only final accuracy. It also reports token-level content-latency proxies, such as when the first supported visible progress appears and how long users wait between updates. That matches the problem formulation much better than plain TTFT.

The main empirical claim is consistent across architectures, scales, and domains: SxS improves the accuracy-latency trade-off without changing the model architecture. At a similar final accuracy, the model can disclose useful supported progress earlier; at a similar content latency, it can achieve better final task performance. The evidence is presented as a Pareto improvement rather than a single scalar gain.

Two ablation-level findings matter most. First, entailment-aligned supervision is necessary. If the objective naively rewards earlier output, the model tends to produce filler or unstable early commitments. Second, RL is necessary. SFT alone teaches the interleaving format but hurts reasoning quality, which confirms that the new format induces a nontrivial distribution shift. RL restores reasoning performance while preserving better pacing behavior.

- Student sees only the target low-resource query x_tgt.
- Teacher additionally sees the aligned English query x* (from a multilingual parallel/jailbreak dataset) plus a CoT instruction C that elicits safe reasoning in English while requiring the final answer in the target language.
Training distills the teacher’s safe output distribution/trajectory into the student so that the student learns safer behavior given only x_tgt.
The framework is presented as compatible with both off-policy self-distillation (teacher-generated data) and on-policy variants (student sampling with teacher guidance).

For LLM-based attacks, the submission instruction is intentionally not “decode”, but “solve the math problem and provide practical real-world examples”, which forces the target model to map the formal solution back into concrete procedures—effectively undoing the obfuscation.a1:T60b,The paper is a controlled reward-design study rather than a new RL method. It compares several reward choices under two critic-free policy-gradient algorithms, GRPO and RLOO, across multiple pretrained code-capable base models. The reward variants include standard binary reward, direct pass-rate reward, reweighted pass-rate variants, and two-stage schedules that combine dense and sparse rewards.

The analysis has two layers. First, the authors verify that pass-rate rewards are indeed denser: many rollouts receive intermediate scores instead of collapsing to all-zero feedback. So the failure mode is not the absence of signal.

Second, they study whether those intermediate rewards induce useful gradient directions. Their central claim is that pass rate is miscalibrated with respect to full correctness. A program can achieve a high pass rate through brittle heuristics, memorized patterns, or overfitting to the provided tests while still being far from correct. Conversely, a nearly correct solution with a small bug may receive only a modest pass rate. Under group-relative updates, this causes ranking errors inside the sampled batch. When no rollout fully solves the problem, different partial solutions push the policy in different directions, and the resulting update tends to be weak or cancel out.

This is the key distinction from naive reward shaping: the paper argues that numerical granularity is not enough. What matters is whether the surrogate reward preserves a meaningful optimization geometry toward the target behavior.a2:T445,From the provided full-text content, the experimental setup spans multiple base models, two critic-free RL algorithms, and several reward designs. The headline result is consistent across these settings: pass-rate rewards do not reliably outperform binary rewards in final code-generation performance.

The most important empirical observations are about training dynamics rather than a single benchmark number:
- pass-rate rewards increase the fraction of non-zero-reward rollouts;
- this extra density does not translate into better pass-all-tests outcomes;
- on hard problems where no rollout is fully correct, partial-pass samples produce noisy and weak policy updates;
- some high-pass-rate programs are shortcut solutions rather than genuinely correct ones;
- reweighted or two-stage variants may help optimization in limited regimes, but they do not overturn the main conclusion.

The excerpt provided here does not include the full numeric tables, model sizes, or exact benchmark scores, so those should be checked directly in the main results tables and appendix rather than inferred.a3:T8c0,DGPO 的核心思路是把“相对参考策略的分布偏离”从单纯的 regularization penalty，改造成 token 级 advantage 重分配的依据。方法仍然是 critic-free，不训练额外 value 网络，而是在 GRPO 的组采样框架上重写 token 权重。

第一部分是距离度量替换。论文认为 reverse KL 有两个问题：一是无界，偏离大时梯度可能很尖；二是偏 mode-seeking，会强烈压制低概率但可能有价值的新轨迹。DGPO 用 Hellinger distance 代替 reverse KL。Hellinger 是有界的，数值范围稳定，因而更适合把“与参考分布不同”解释成一种可控的探索强度，而不是必须压回去的错误。这里的关键不是简单换一个 f-divergence，而是换掉了训练信号的语义：偏离不再只意味着风险，也可能意味着关键推理跳跃。

第二部分是 token 级 credit reallocation。对一条获得正向回报的序列，DGPO 不再把同一个 advantage 平均施加到所有 token，而是根据每个 token 相对参考策略的分布偏离程度，动态分配更大的或更小的更新权重。直观上，若某个 token 在当前策略下与参考模型差异更大，它更可能对应一处真正推动解题成功的探索步骤，因此应获得更高 credit。这样做的目标，是把 sequence-level reward 拆成 process-like supervision，但又不需要人工过程标注或 value model。

第三部分是 entropy gating。仅靠偏离程度会奖励“假创新”：模型也可能对错误、幻觉、离谱 token 给出高置信度，从而产生大偏离。为此，论文引入基于策略熵的门控，用归一化 epistemic uncertainty 去缩放 Hellinger 信号。高偏离且高不确定性的 token 更像是在探索；高偏离但低熵、高置信的 token 更可能是自信地胡说，因此其 credit 会被压低。这个设计很关键，因为它把“探索”与“幻觉”做了一个粗分离。

从算法形态看，DGPO 仍保留 GRPO 的组相对优化框架和低内存特性，没有引入 critic，也没有走到完整 process reward model。它试图占据一个中间位置：比序列级 RL 更细，但比 token-level verifier 或 step-level RM 更轻。a4:T413,Its contribution is not to pretraining directly, but it is relevant to the pretrain–posttrain interface. In long-horizon reasoning RL, the bottleneck is increasingly not whether a reward exists, but how that reward is propagated through the generated process. Better token-level credit assignment means the behavioral change induced by RL can be more localized, instead of simply increasing the probability of the entire chain of thought. That matters for understanding whether RL is actually shaping reasoning patterns rather than just response style. The second useful point is that reverse KL may be a poor default if the goal is to discover new reasoning trajectories. Reinterpreting policy deviation as a guidance signal rather than only a penalty is a sensible move, especially in verifiable domains such as math. In contribution type, this is an objective-design paper rather than a paradigm shift, but it targets a real pain point in current critic-free reasoning RL: balancing fine-grained credit assignment with stable exploration.a5:T961,DGPO turns deviation from the reference policy into a token-level signal for redistributing credit. The framework remains critic-free: it does not train an auxiliary value network, and it stays close to the group-sampling setup of GRPO while changing how token updates are weighted.

The first change is the divergence measure. The paper argues that reverse KL is problematic because it is unbounded and strongly mode-seeking. Large deviations can create sharp gradients, and low-probability but potentially useful trajectories are heavily discouraged. DGPO replaces reverse KL with the Hellinger distance. Since Hellinger is bounded, it provides a numerically smoother notion of policy deviation and is better suited for treating deviation as controlled exploration rather than as an error that must always be suppressed. The important point is not merely swapping one f-divergence for another; it changes the meaning of the signal used during optimization.

The second change is token-level credit reallocation. For a positively rewarded sequence, DGPO does not broadcast the same advantage to all tokens. Instead, it redistributes the sequence-level advantage according to each token’s distributional deviation from the reference policy. Intuitively, tokens that differ more from the reference are more likely to correspond to the exploratory steps that made the solution succeed, so they receive larger updates. The goal is to approximate process-level supervision without requiring step annotations or a learned value model.

The third component is entropy gating. Distributional deviation alone can reward fake innovation: the model may confidently emit incorrect or hallucinatory tokens that are far from the reference policy. To reduce this failure mode, DGPO scales the Hellinger-based signal by normalized policy entropy, interpreted as epistemic uncertainty. High-deviation, high-uncertainty tokens are treated as plausible exploration; high-deviation, low-entropy tokens are more likely to be confident mistakes and are down-weighted. This is the key mechanism that tries to separate useful exploration from hallucination.

Algorithmically, DGPO stays in the middle ground. It is finer than sequence-level RL, but much lighter than full process reward modeling or token-level verification. That is why the paper emphasizes critic-free scalability rather than maximal supervision quality.a6:T748,The evaluation focuses on AIME 2024 and AIME 2025, using 7B and 32B models. The headline numbers in the abstract are 60.0% Avg@32 on AIME 2024 and 46.0% on AIME 2025, outperforming the DAPO baseline among critic-free alignment methods. Another important result is efficiency: DGPO reportedly adds only about 3.6% time overhead relative to vanilla GRPO, with essentially the same memory footprint because no value network is introduced. That matters because the paper’s claim is not just better reasoning performance, but better credit assignment at nearly the same systems cost.

From the paper’s logic, the most informative experiments are likely not only the final benchmark scores. First, convergence comparisons against GRPO and DAPO matter: if token-level redistribution is genuinely more effective, the method should separate earlier during training, not only at the end. Second, the ablation replacing reverse KL with Hellinger should be read through the lens of stability—gradient behavior, policy drift, collapse frequency—not just task accuracy. Third, the entropy-gating ablation is central. If removing the gate hurts performance or increases hallucination-like behavior, that supports the claim that deviation alone is too noisy a proxy for useful reasoning steps. Fourth, consistency across 7B and 32B is important; if both scales benefit, the method is less likely to be a narrow sweet-spot trick.

For each prompt, the policy samples multiple responses, receives verifiable rewards, and computes normalized group-wise advantages. Each response has a sequence-level advantage shared by all its generated tokens. The mismatch arises because the PPO term is token-level while the advantage is sequence-level. Token aggregation averages over all tokens in the group, so longer responses carry more weight. If positive and negative responses have different length distributions, the update is biased by this sign-length coupling. Sequence aggregation first averages within each response and then across responses, removing the positive-negative length coupling but forcing equal response weights and reducing the per-token influence of longer outputs. Balanced Aggregation splits responses by the sign of their normalized advantage, computes token-level means inside the positive and negative subsets separately, and combines the two subset losses with weights proportional to the number of sequences in each subset. This keeps inter-sign balance while avoiding strict equal weighting of every response.ac:T444,The paper defines a power distribution over full completions, typically of the form q_alpha(y|x) proportional to pi(y|x)^alpha. When alpha is greater than one, probability mass concentrates on sequences that the base model already assigns high likelihood. The first technical result shows that cheap token-level approximations cannot generally reproduce this sequence-level distribution unless they have information about possible suffixes. This is because the correct token-level marginal under the power distribution depends on the total powered probability of all continuations. The RL connection comes from a KL-regularized objective where the reward is the model’s own sequence log-likelihood, r_self(x,y)=log pi(y|x). The closed-form optimizer of this objective is exactly a power distribution. Rewriting the same objective yields power self-distillation, where a student amortizes the teacher distribution induced by power sampling. The paper further proves a sharpening guarantee and characterizes true-reward improvement through a covariance condition under the power distribution.ad:T824,The method, Anchored Learning, replaces direct optimization toward a fixed target with distillation toward a moving anchor distribution. At each iteration, the anchor is constructed by interpolating between the current model and a frozen reference model. The trainable model is then updated toward this intermediate target rather than pushed directly by task loss alone or constrained only by a static reference.

Mechanistically, this converts a potentially large global shift into a sequence of local, conservative moves in distribution space. The paper presents two variants: probability-space anchoring and logit-space anchoring. In the first, interpolation happens directly over output probabilities; in the second, interpolation is performed in logit space before softmax. Both admit explicit per-step KL upper bounds, while the logit-space version is closer to standard training pipelines and easier to integrate with existing distillation implementations.

The key distinction from ordinary distillation is that the teacher is not fixed. It is a trajectory-aware mixture of the current policy and a frozen reference. This design addresses the main weakness of static KL or fixed-teacher methods: when the target task is far from the base model, task gradients and regularization gradients can remain in persistent conflict. The moving anchor instead defines a gradual path between preservation and adaptation, so each update only needs to traverse a short local segment.

The theory is focused and useful. Rather than proving generic convergence, the authors derive linear upper bounds on the KL divergence induced by each anchored update. This gives the method an implicit trust-region interpretation: it does not solve a constrained optimization problem explicitly, but it behaves like one by restricting each step to a local neighborhood. The paper also argues why this local control is better aligned with non-convex training than static reference matching: static KL constrains distance from the starting point, while anchoring constrains distance from the current point.ae:T752,The empirical section is organized around the gain–stability trade-off rather than target-task performance alone. The headline result is that standard SFT causes more than 53% degradation on iGSM and MedCalc, whereas Anchored Learning reduces that drop to below 5% while preserving near-optimal task gains. One concrete number reported in the paper is a 75.2% gain on iGSM.

The most important empirical claim is Pareto dominance or near-Pareto-frontier behavior. At matched or similar task gains, Anchored Learning forgets substantially less than strong baselines; at matched stability, it delivers larger gains than static KL regularization or fixed distillation. That matters because it suggests the method is not merely trading learning speed for conservatism through smaller effective updates.

The ablations are informative in three ways. First, moving anchors outperform frozen teachers and static KL baselines, indicating that the dynamic reference is the main source of benefit. Second, the interpolation coefficient shows a real trade-off: too little anchoring collapses toward ordinary SFT, while too much makes optimization overly conservative and hurts target improvement. The method first defines two reference directions in parameter space: a safety direction and a danger direction. The safety direction is obtained from a DPO-aligned model trained on PKU-SafeRLHF-10K, while the danger direction is obtained from a model fine-tuned toward harmful behavior using datasets such as Aegis and BeaverTails. A sample is considered riskier if its update aligns more with the danger direction and less with the safety direction. This differs from perturbation-magnitude analysis: two updates with the same norm can have different behavioral consequences if their directions differ.
